analysis.one_liner: Exempts farm and logging stormwater runoff from Clean Water Act pollution permits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have lifted Clean Water Act permit requirements for agricultural and forestry runoff, died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Clean Water Act so that the EPA could not require water pollution permits for runoff from farms, pastures, orchards, aquaculture facilities, and forestry operations. It would also stop the EPA from pressuring states to require those permits, and would remove agricultural stormwater, irrigation return flows, and logging stormwater from the law's definition of a pollution "point source" [S3]. In practice, discharges carrying soil, fertilizer, pesticide, and logging-debris runoff would flow without federal discharge permits or state equivalents [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Farming, ranching, aquaculture, and timber operators would gain if the bill passed: they would avoid the cost and paperwork of discharge permits for their stormwater and forestry runoff [S2] [S3]. Timber companies would be the clearest winners, since the bill exempts every stage of logging — harvesting, road building and maintenance, site preparation, drainage, and pest and fire control — from permit requirements [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA from requiring a discharge permit for discharges composed entirely of agricultural stormwater, including runoff from crops, pastures, rangeland, orchards, aquaculture facilities, and forest land [S3] [S2].

Bars the EPA from requiring permits for discharges from silviculture (forestry) operations, defined broadly to include nurseries, reforestation, thinning, prescribed burning, harvesting, site preparation, road construction and maintenance, drainage, and pest and fire control [S3].
Prohibits the EPA from directly or indirectly requiring states to impose those permits, closing the route by which the agency has influenced state permitting programs [S3].

Rewrites the Clean Water Act's definition of "point source" so agricultural stormwater, irrigation return flows, and logging stormwater no longer count as pollution sources covered by the permit system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Downstream communities and water users would bear the cost if it passed: more runoff carrying sediment, fertilizer, and pesticides would enter rivers and lakes without permit limits, and downstream utilities and towns would face higher treatment costs and dirtier water. The EPA and state water agencies would also lose a regulatory tool [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill removes agricultural and forestry runoff from the permit system entirely and even bars the EPA from indirectly pressuring states to regulate it, which would leave that runoff — a known carrier of sediment, nutrients, and pesticides — without discharge limits [S3] [S2].

By striking agricultural stormwater, irrigation return flows, and silviculture stormwater from the legal definition of a "point source," the bill would shrink the reach of the Clean Water Act itself, not just one EPA program [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the fairness argument behind the bill — that treating diffuse farm and forest runoff like pipe discharges is burdensome — but the bill answers that by exempting entire categories of discharge, including logging road construction and drainage, rather than by easing permit rules for small operations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is real for farm and timber operators: discharge permits cost money and time, and runoff from fields and forests is not the same as pollution from a pipe. But the way the bill is written, it would exempt whole industries' runoff from the Clean Water Act's permit system — including logging roads and drainage, which are major sediment sources — and would tie the EPA's hands with states as well. The water-quality cost would land on downstream communities, fisheries, and water suppliers. On balance, the bill's exemptions are broader than the fairness problem it is trying to solve.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Hutchinson introduced it in March 2000 and it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Hutchinson introduced the Timber and Agriculture Environmental Fairness Act on March 2, 2000, with Senator Michael Enzi [S1] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; no further committee or floor action ever followed [S5].
The bill had only two Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without the bill receiving a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who drink water, fish, and recreate downstream came out ahead: the Clean Water Act's permit requirements for farm and logging runoff stayed intact because the bill never moved. Farm and timber operators who wanted permit exemptions are worse off than they would have been under the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; the only three senators involved — the sponsor and two cosponsors — were all Republicans [S4] [S1].

industries.note: The bill would exempt every stage of forestry — harvesting, road construction and maintenance, site preparation, drainage, and pest and fire control — from Clean Water Act discharge permits [S3]. Logging roads and site work are major sources of sediment in streams, so the cost of the exemption falls on downstream water users [S2] [S3].

The bill would bar permits for agricultural stormwater from crops, pastures, rangeland, orchards, and aquaculture, and would also exclude irrigation return flows from the point-source definition [S3]. Operators would save permit costs while fertilizer and pesticide runoff flows unpermitted.
With upstream farm and logging runoff unpermitted, downstream water systems would face higher sediment and nutrient loads and greater treatment costs [S2] [S3].
